qs.q: A 33-year-old woman with a history of endometriosis is undergoing laparoscopic surgery. The surgeon identifies a 2 cm endometrioma on the right ovary. What is the most appropriate surgical management to preserve fertility?
o: Oophorectomy performed to prevent any future recurrence of the cyst
Cystectomy executed with careful dissection to preserve ovarian tissue
Aspiration of the cyst contents performed under ultrasound guidance
Windowing of the cyst performed to drain the chocolate-colored fluid
Contralateral cystectomy performed to address the other pathology
qs.e: Cystectomy preserves ovarian reserve better than oophorectomy or aspiration.

qs.q: A 32-year-old woman with a history of endometriosis is undergoing IVF. Her anti-Müllerian hormone level is 0.8 ng/mL. What does this result suggest about her ovarian reserve?
o: Indicates normal ovarian reserve with an expected adequate response to stimulation.
Suggests polycystic ovary syndrome and a high likelihood of strong response.
Predicts a high ovarian response, increasing risk of hyperstimulation syndrome.
Reflects premature ovarian failure, implying minimal or no response to stimulation.
Denotes diminished ovarian reserve, indicating possible poor response to stimulation.
qs.e: Low AMH levels indicate diminished ovarian reserve and poor response to IVF.

qs.q: A 30‑year‑old woman with chronic pelvic pain, dysmenorrhoea and dyspareunia has a normal pelvic examination. Which imaging modality is best for mapping possible endometriosis?
o: Transvaginal ultrasound
Magnetic resonance imaging
Computed tomography of the abdomen
Plain radiography
qs.e: MRI provides detailed soft‑tissue contrast useful for delineating endometriotic lesions. Ultrasound is less sensitive for deep infiltrating disease, and CT or X‑ray are not appropriate.

qs.q: A 28-year-old woman undergoes pelvic surgery for severe endometriosis and wishes to minimize the subsequent risk of post-operative adhesion formation affecting her future fertility. Which anti-adhesion barrier film can be placed intraoperatively?
o: Polypropylene surgical mesh
Hyaluronate-carboxymethylcellulose film
Polytetrafluoroethylene vascular patch
Oxidized cellulose hemostatic gauze
qs.e: Hyaluronate-carboxymethylcellulose film (Seprafilm) and oxidised regenerated cellulose (Interceed) are established anti-adhesion barriers used to reduce adhesion formation. Polypropylene mesh is a permanent foreign material that induces significant scarring.
qs.s: Thoracic Outlet Syndrome, Peritoneal Adhesions and Compartment: MCQs

qs.q: Which theory of endometriosis pathogenesis proposes that menstrual endometrium flows backward through the fallopian tubes to implant on pelvic structures?
o: Vascular dissemination theory
Coelomic metaplasia theory
Retrograde menstruation theory
Induction theory mechanism
qs.e: Sampson's theory of retrograde menstruation is the most widely accepted mechanism for the development of pelvic endometriosis. Other theories involve coelomic metaplasia or lymphatic dissemination, but retrograde flow accounts for most common pelvic sites.
qs.s: Female & Male Genital Pathology: Ulcers, HPV, Endometriosis,: MCQs

qs.q: Adenomyosis differs from endometriosis in that adenomyosis
o: Forms chocolate cysts within the ovarian parenchyma
Involves functioning endometrium that bleeds cyclically
Derives from the basalis layer and does not bleed cyclically
Commonly affects distant sites like the lungs and bone
qs.e: Adenomyosis derives from the stratum basalis which does not respond to hormonal cycling. Endometriosis contains functioning endometrium that undergoes cyclic bleeding.

qs.q: Which theory of endometriosis best explains its occurrence in the lungs and skeletal muscle?
o: Retrograde menstruation through fallopian tubes
Metaplastic transformation of coelomic epithelium
Direct implantation during surgical procedures
Vascular or lymphatic dissemination of endometrial cells
qs.e: Vascular and lymphatic dissemination explains how endometrial tissue reaches distant sites like the lungs, heart, and skeletal muscle where retrograde flow cannot reach.

qs.q: Why are COX-2 inhibitors and aromatase inhibitors useful in treating endometriosis?
o: They reduce prostaglandin E2 and local oestrogen production
They block HPV-related proliferation of endometrial cells
They stimulate progesterone receptors in the myometrium
They directly destroy ectopic endometrial implants surgically
qs.e: Endometriotic tissue has high aromatase activity and elevated PGE2, promoting local oestrogen and survival of ectopic tissue. Both drug classes target these mechanisms.

ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: Endometriosis is the presence of functional endometrial tissue outside the uterus, causing chronic pelvic pain and infertility. Diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion, imaging, and sometimes laparoscopy.

sections.p: Endometriosis is ectopic endometrial glands and stroma that respond to hormonal cycles, producing inflammation and scarring.
b: Definitive diagnosis: visualisation of lesions and histology on laparoscopy
Probable diagnosis: typical pain pattern + pelvic ultrasound showing ovarian endometrioma

t.b: Does the patient have an ovarian cyst with ‘ground‑glass’ echogenicity? Positive suggests endometrioma; negative does not rule out peritoneal disease.
Is deep infiltrating disease present? Helpful for mapping lesions when ultrasound is inconclusive.
Can the lesions be visualised and sampled? Gold standard; confirms diagnosis.

sections.p: The revised American Society for Reproductive Medicine (rASRM) system grades disease from I (minimal) to IV (severe) based on lesion size, depth, and adhesions.
b: Stage I–II: superficial implants, small endometriomas
Stage III–IV: deep infiltrating lesions, large endometriomas, extensive adhesions

sections.p: Exact cause is unknown; several mechanisms contribute.
b: Retrograde menstruation – most common hypothesis
Coelomic metaplasia – peritoneal cells transform
Vascular/lymphatic spread – explains distant lesions

sections.p: Symptoms vary with lesion location and hormonal phase.
b: Dysmenorrhea worsening over time
Chronic pelvic pain unrelated to menses
Dyspareunia, especially deep penetration
Infertility despite normal ovulation

sections.p: Select tests that answer specific clinical questions.

t.b: Is there a marker of disease activity? May be modestly elevated; normal does not exclude disease.
Is ovulation occurring? Helps assess infertility work‑up; low levels suggest anovulation, not endometriosis.

sections.p: Complications arise from deep infiltrating disease and adhesions.
b: Bowel obstruction from rectovaginal nodules
Hydroureter or renal impairment from ureteral involvement
Severe anemia from chronic menstrual loss

sections.p: Treat pain, preserve fertility, and limit disease progression.
b: Hormonal suppression – combined oral contraceptives, progestins, GnRH agonists; chosen to create a hypo‑estrogenic state and reduce lesion activity.
NSAIDs – first‑line for dysmenorrhea; avoid in renal disease or active ulcer.
Surgical excision – laparoscopy to remove implants and restore anatomy; preferred for deep disease or infertility.
Fertility treatment – IVF after optimal disease control; surgery may improve spontaneous conception.

sections.p: Long‑term monitoring is needed because recurrence is common.
b: Review pain and menstrual pattern every 6 months
Repeat imaging if symptoms change
Consider hormonal maintenance after surgery to lower recurrence

sections.p: Conditions that mimic endometriosis pain or imaging findings.
b: Adenomyosis – diffuse uterine enlargement, similar dysmenorrhea
Pelvic inflammatory disease – pain with fever, discharge
Ovarian cysts (functional) – unilateral pain without typical endometrioma features

sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely reassuring.
b: Normal CA‑125 does not exclude disease, especially early stage
Ultrasound may miss superficial peritoneal implants

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe abdominal pain suggesting bowel obstruction
Acute urinary retention or flank pain indicating ureteral obstruction
Heavy menstrual bleeding causing hemodynamic instability
